customManagers.description: The pin of the 8.8 bugfix line.
The pin of the 8.9 bugfix line.

The pin of the current-GA line, which is also the default of a plain build. It was the preview line until Camunda released 8.10.0 on 2026-09-29. A preview line pins a pre-release, so it also needed a rule keeping it off a candidate of an alpha such as 8.10.0-alpha5-rc2, which is a step towards an alpha rather than something to publish a line on. This pin is a release now and Renovate offers no pre-release against one, so that rule went with the preview line and the next preview line needs it again.

packageRules.description: VanillaBP and the adapters follow the framework, not Renovate: their versions are bumped when a release is cut, and while they are snapshots there is nothing to look up.

Netty is not ours to raise. The Quarkus platform manages a Netty version and ships GraalVM substitutions written against exactly it; a newer minor breaks the native image with 'Could not find target method' on a Netty class the substitution targets, while every JVM test stays green - which is how 4.2.17 got here. The property follows the Quarkus version, and it is raised by hand together with it.

Protobuf arrives with the Camunda client and stays on the version that client generated its code against. The property exists to beat the Spring Boot BOM, not to be the newest one available: an application whose protocol classes were generated by another gencode version fails with an ExceptionInInitializerError on the first command. It is raised by hand when a client pin moves, and Camunda8ProtobufPinTest fails the build of the line whose client asks for more than the pin gives.

The client pins are maintained by the custom managers above, one per line. Renovate's own maven manager sees the same dependency a second time through the dependencyManagement entry and would open a second pull request for a property one of those managers already owns.

Every line keeps its own pin, so a client update is proposed per line rather than as one shared PR: the lines are released separately and a failure on one must not hold up a bugfix on another. A patch and a minor are separated here rather than repository-wide, because for these pins the two mean different things: upkeep inside the line, and a new line.

A patch of the client stays inside the line: the minimum cluster version is the minor, and a patch does not move it. That makes this ordinary upkeep, and the build proves it against a real cluster of that line, so it merges itself once the checks passed.
prBodyNotes: A client brings generated protobuf code, and protobuf refuses a runtime older than its gencode. If this bump raises what the client asks for, `<protobuf.version>` in `pom.xml` has to move with it. `Camunda8ProtobufPinTest` fails this build with both numbers when it does, so a red check here is the answer rather than a mystery.

packageRules.description: While a pin names a pre-release, nothing proposed for it merges itself. Renovate reads the step from the last candidate of a minor to its release as a patch: major, minor and patch stay the same and only the qualifier falls away. The rule above would therefore have merged that step as soon as its checks were green. The pin is the small part of it. A line pins a pre-release while it is the preview line, and reaching the release is the moment that line becomes a GA line, which also moves the line table of the README, the camunda8.line.preview property of the line profile, the question whether the oldest line is still carried, and the release of the line itself. The condition is the current value of the pin, so nothing has to state a second time which line is the preview one. It is written as 'not a plain three-number release' rather than as a list of the qualifiers Camunda uses today, so a qualifier nobody has seen yet lands on the careful side. The lines are matched by a pattern and not by name, because a line added later would otherwise fall back into the automerge and nobody would hear about it. renovate/verify-pin-automerge.js checks what this rule does, with Renovate's own classifier and rule engine.
prBodyNotes: The pin this starts from names a pre-release, so nothing here merges itself. Where this is the step onto the release of that minor, the line stops being the preview line with it. Part of the same move are the line table of the `README.md` and of the wiki, the `camunda8.line.preview` property of the `line-*` profile, whether the oldest line is still carried, and the release of the line.

packageRules.description: A minor of the client is a new line, not an update. The client a build was compiled against is the lowest cluster version that build accepts, so this bump raises the cluster requirement of everybody who consumes the line. It gets a branch of its own, waits for approval on the dependency dashboard and never merges itself. Rotating the lines is more than this pin: it also means a profile, the pin properties, the line table of the README and a release of the new line.
prBodyNotes: A client brings generated protobuf code, and protobuf refuses a runtime older than its gencode. If this bump raises what the client asks for, `<protobuf.version>` in `pom.xml` has to move with it. `Camunda8ProtobufPinTest` fails this build with both numbers when it does.

This crosses a release-line boundary. A Camunda 8 cluster and the applications running on it move together, and a cluster upgrade costs more organizationally than technically, which is why the lines exist at all. Merging this raises the lowest cluster version the built artifacts accept.
Before merging: is the new minor GA, does the line table of the README still describe reality, and is the oldest line still carried?
